deepSky.name: Pleiades

info.basic: The Pleiades is the most famous open star cluster in the sky, a tight knot of hot blue stars in Taurus that most people can pick out with the naked eye and count six or seven of. It sits about 444 light-years away and is only around 100 million years old.
info.scientific: M45 is a young open cluster of B-type stars roughly 136 parsecs (444 light-years) distant, per Gaia DR3 and VLBI parallax measurements; earlier Hipparcos measurements of about 118 pc were disputed and superseded. Its brightest members share a common origin and motion, and the reflection nebulosity seen around Merope and Maia is an unrelated interstellar dust cloud the cluster is currently passing through, not leftover material from its own formation.

deepSky.sources: Wikipedia, Pleiades (star cluster); Gaia DR3 (2023) parallax 135.74±0.10 pc; van Leeuwen VLBI (2014) 136.2±1.2 pc

info.basic: The Crab Nebula is the wreckage of a star that exploded as a supernova in the year 1054, an event bright enough to be recorded by astronomers in China and elsewhere. At its heart spins the crushed core of that star, a neutron star flashing 30 times a second.
info.scientific: M1 is a pulsar wind nebula and supernova remnant about 6,500 light-years away, roughly 970 years old, spanning some 6 by 4 arcminutes (about 11 light-years across) and still expanding. Its filamentary shell of ionised ejecta (H, He, C, O, N, Fe, Ne, S at 11,000-18,000 K) surrounds a diffuse blue core produced by synchrotron radiation from relativistic electrons accelerated by the Crab Pulsar's magnetic field, not by ongoing star formation.
